proposals.relationship: Kerber uses Geertz’s account of common sense as culturally filled with presuppositions to explain the persuasive power of separate-spheres language.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 essay, 11/n2, quotes Local Knowledge (1983),84, in explaining how the trope shaped historians’ selections and readers’ expectations. This is a specific analytical resource, not adoption of Geertz’s entire anthropology or an exclusive formative influence. The cited original remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Kerber draws on Arendt’s analysis of the Greek public/private distinction to extend the history of gendered spheres beyond nineteenth-century America.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 discussion, 18–19/n19, explicitly credits The Human Condition (1958),22–78, especially24/72, for the contrast between biological necessity and public action. Kerber examines a historically gendered exclusion; this does not endorse Greek prescriptions or Arendt’s complete political theory. Aristotle is separately cited through Benjamin Jowett’s translation, with Judith Hallett credited for that reference; Okin’s different resource remains separate. Originals unread.
primary_locators: 1988 printed 18 paragraph beginning The distinction between the private and the public, continued19; note19.

proposals.relationship: Kerber uses Hayden White’s warning about discourse exceeding its evidence to illuminate the ambiguity and historical usefulness of separate-spheres language.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed30/n41 links the trope’s hidden instrumentality and ambiguity to a substantial quotation from Tropics of Discourse (1978),1, on tensions between data and organizing consciousness. The named writer is Hayden White, not Deborah Gray White, who appears elsewhere in the essay. This specific rhetorical resource does not claim full agreement with White’s narrative theory; original unread.
primary_locators: 1988 printed30 paragraph beginning Historians of working women and note41.

proposals.relationship: Kerber points to Scott’s analysis of gender as a resource for understanding political systems and gender relations as reciprocal social constructions.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 final paragraph and note55 identify Scott’s Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986),1053–1075, as an especially valuable analysis for the argument. Montesquieu’s Persian Letters through C.J.Betts and Spirit of the Laws through Thomas Nugent, plus Michael Shapiro, receive their distinct credit. This does not infer Derrida’s or Lévi-Strauss’s personal influence from the essay’s generic deconstruction language. Scott’s original remains unread here.

proposals.relationship: Kerber draws on Ryan’s account of family strategies and class formation to show how women’s separate sphere could support household mobility while limiting women’s own autonomy.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed24–25/n29 substantively discusses Cradle of the Middle Class (1981), especially56/185, in relation to paid women’s work, sons’ education and family interests. Printed37/n49 separately credits Ryan’s forthcoming urban-public-space work, without treating a later published version as already read; printed9 acknowledges Ryan’s counsel on drafts among many other readers. These specific uses do not establish exclusive influence, formal mentoring or agreement with every Ryan conclusion. Ryan originals and drafts unread.
primary_locators: 1988 printed24 second and third paragraphs, continued25; note29;37/n49;9 author acknowledgment.

proposals.relationship: Kerber expressly credits Higginbotham’s interpretation of race as a resource for her discussion of Black women and the separate-spheres framework.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed26/n30 acknowledges an interpretive debt to Evelyn Brooks, The Problem of Race in Women’s History, alongside separately credited work by the Hortons, Sterling, Jones and Deborah Gray White. Higginbotham’s own Harvard CV establishes the identity through that distinctive chapter title and editor; metadata does not itself establish the debt. Kerber’s forthcoming volume title is preserved, not silently replaced with the later 1989 title. Printed9 also thanks Evelyn Brooks for counsel on earlier drafts, among many colleagues; no individual task or final chapter edition is inferred. Higginbotham chapter itself unread.
primary_locators: 1988 printed25 final sentence continued26 first paragraph and note30;9 author acknowledgment; Higginbotham CV PDF1 heading/PDF2 publication list.

proposals.relationship: Kerber credits Faust with counsel on earlier versions of her essay on separate-spheres rhetoric.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 author acknowledgment at9 names Drew Faust in a larger group of advisors. The credit concerns this particular essay’s earlier versions; it does not specify which passage Faust influenced, assign sole responsibility for a concept, establish formal mentoring or imply Faust endorsed all conclusions. Kerber retains responsibility for remaining errors. No independent manuscript correspondence read.
primary_locators: 1988 printed9 author acknowledgment beginning I am deeply grateful for the good counsel.

proposals.relationship: Kerber uses Thompson’s account of industrial time discipline to distinguish changing work patterns among women and men.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed23 explicitly treats factory and school employment as entry into a clock-measured work regime given classic formulation by E.P.Thompson. Printed16/n14 supplies the 1967 essay citation and separately explains Cott’s extension to married women’s household tasks. The current Thompson-to-Cott edge2087 and Cott-to-Kerber edge2094 already record that distinct adaptation; this proposal concerns Kerber’s additional direct use in her comparison of women’s work regimes. Hareven and Dublin retain their separate empirical/interpretive credit; no fresh Thompson original or Cott book read.
primary_locators: 1988 printed23 paragraph beginning In Motz’s Michigan, especially sentence When women worked in factories;note27 at23;16/n14 identifies Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism (1967).

proposals.relationship: Kerber credits Hofstadter’s example with teaching her to ask consequential questions, choose her own research problem and connect historical understanding to political understanding.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2020 lecture2 and8 explains particular lessons, his readings seminar and approval of her dissertation prospectus. She also remembers his resistance to being called a consensus historian and his preference for skeptic, and says the book and conversation may have lodged in her thinking. Graduate peers share credit for the history/politics lesson; Lerner later supplied distinct mentoring after Hofstadter’s early death. This is explicit retrospective formation, not an inference solely from supervision or a claim that Hofstadter originated her later feminism. His original works and her dissertation unread.
primary_locators: 2020 Haskins lecture printed2 opening;8 Columbia section;9 opening paragraph;14–15 on later recognition of omissions.
